mcq.explanation: Kubernetes is primarily used for orchestrating containerized applications: it schedules containers across machines, keeps the desired number running, restarts failed ones, and handles service discovery, scaling and rolling updates.
mcq.distractors: It is not a version-control, photo-editing or kernel-build tool.

mcq.explanation: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit, containing one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP) and can share volumes. Kubernetes schedules Pods, not individual containers.
mcq.distractors: A Terraform provider, a data center and an image registry are all outside Kubernetes' object model.

mcq.explanation: etcd is the consistent, distributed key-value store that holds all cluster state (objects, specs, status). Only the API server talks to it directly, which is why etcd backups are critical.
mcq.distractors: containerd runs containers, CoreDNS serves cluster DNS and kube-proxy programs Service routing; none of them store cluster state.

mcq.explanation: kube-scheduler watches for Pods with no node assigned and picks a node based on resource requests, affinity, taints/tolerations and other constraints, then records the binding via the API server.
mcq.distractors: kube-proxy handles Service networking, kubectl is a client CLI, and the kubelet runs Pods after they are already assigned.

mcq.explanation: The kubelet is the node agent that ensures Pod containers run on a node: it watches the API server for Pods bound to its node, starts them through the container runtime (CRI), runs probes and reports status back.
mcq.distractors: Cluster state lives in etcd; Helm charts and pull requests have nothing to do with the kubelet.

mcq.explanation: kubectl is a CLI for interacting with the Kubernetes API: every `kubectl get/apply/describe` becomes an HTTPS request to the kube-apiserver using credentials from your kubeconfig.
mcq.distractors: It is not a filesystem, protocol or image format.

mcq.explanation: `kubectl get pods` lists Pods in the current namespace (add `-A` for all namespaces, `-o wide` for node and IP).
mcq.distractors: `kubectl show`, `kubectl list` and `kubectl build` are not kubectl verbs; the read verb is `get`.

mcq.explanation: A namespace is a logical grouping for cluster resources inside one cluster: names must be unique per namespace, and RBAC, ResourceQuotas and policies can be scoped to it.
mcq.distractors: It is not a Dockerfile instruction, an image tag, or physical isolation on a dedicated server.

mcq.explanation: kube-apiserver exposes the Kubernetes API: it is the front door that authenticates, authorises and validates requests and is the only component that reads and writes etcd.
mcq.distractors: The kubelet is a node agent, CoreDNS serves DNS and kube-proxy handles Service traffic.

mcq.explanation: A worker node is a machine (VM or physical) that runs application Pods; it runs the kubelet, a container runtime and usually kube-proxy, while the control plane manages it.
mcq.distractors: DNS records, workflow files and Helm repositories are not compute machines.

checks.label: Checks the cluster connection (cluster-info / config current-context)

labs.modelAnswer:
kubectl config current-context     # which cluster/user kubeconfig points at
kubectl cluster-info               # API server URL and CoreDNS endpoint
kubectl get nodes -o wide          # nodes, Ready status, roles, version, internal IP, OS, runtime
kubectl describe node <node-name>  # capacity/allocatable, conditions, taints, Pods on the node
kubectl get namespaces             # default, kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease (+ your own)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system    # control-plane and add-on Pods (coredns, kube-proxy, etcd, ...)
kubectl get all -A                 # Pods, Services, Deployments, ReplicaSets in every namespace
kubectl api-resources              # every resource type the API serves, short names, namespaced or not
labs.explanation: Tests basic cluster navigation with kubectl and understanding of what the output means. A good answer confirms which context it is connected to, shows nodes are Ready, lists the default namespaces, and inspects resources across namespaces, with a short note on each command. Watch for confusing namespaced resources (Pods) with cluster-scoped ones (Nodes, Namespaces).

checks.label: Deploys the app (kubectl create deployment / apply)
Confirms a healthy state (rollout status / Running / Ready)

labs.modelAnswer:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=2
kubectl rollout status deployment/web        # waits until "successfully rolled out"
kubectl get deployments,pods -l app=web -o wide
# Expect: READY 2/2, Pods STATUS Running, RESTARTS 0
kubectl describe deployment web               # replicas, strategy, conditions (Available=True)
kubectl describe pod -l app=web               # Events: Scheduled, Pulling, Pulled, Created, Started
kubectl logs deployment/web                   # nginx startup messages
kubectl logs -l app=web --tail=20
labs.explanation: Tests deploying a workload and the three core inspection commands. Check that the Deployment reports all replicas ready, the Pods are Running with no restarts, the describe Events show a clean schedule/pull/start sequence, and logs show the app started. `kubectl rollout status` or `kubectl wait --for=condition=Available` is the cleanest health confirmation.

labs.modelAnswer:
[kubectl] --HTTPS--> +---------------- Control plane ----------------+
                       |  kube-apiserver  <---->  etcd                 |
                       |     ^      ^                                  |
                       |     |      |                                  |
                       |  kube-scheduler   kube-controller-manager     |
                       +-----|-------------------------------------------+
                             | watch / status
              +--------------v-------------+   +------------------------+
              | Worker node 1              |   | Worker node 2          |
              | kubelet -> containerd      |   | kubelet -> containerd  |
              | kube-proxy, Pods           |   | kube-proxy, Pods       |
              +----------------------------+   +------------------------+

kubectl: client CLI; sends requests to the API server using kubeconfig credentials.
kube-apiserver: front door of the cluster; authenticates, validates, and is the only component that reads/writes etcd.
etcd: consistent key-value store holding all cluster state (desired and observed).
kube-scheduler: assigns unscheduled Pods to nodes based on resources and constraints.
kube-controller-manager: runs control loops (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node, Job...) that drive actual state toward desired state.
kubelet: agent on every node; starts Pods' containers via the container runtime, runs probes, reports status.
labs.explanation: Tests the control-plane vs node split and how components talk. Key points to verify: everything goes through the API server (no component other than it touches etcd), the scheduler only decides placement, controllers reconcile desired state, and the kubelet actually runs containers on each node. kubectl is just a client of the API.
